Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed real-world CSF classification study•October 22, 2026

AA-2024 nearly doubled CSF-defined biological AD in one clinic

Among 146 consecutive tertiary-clinic patients, AA-2024 classified 49.3% as biological AD versus 27.4% under AT(N) 2018; all 32 reclassifications moved from non-AD to AD despite lower tau burden and heterogeneous clinical diagnoses.

Key quantitative results: AT(N) 2018 classified 40/146 patients (27.4%) as biological AD, compared with 72/146 (49.3%) under AA-2024.

BiomarkersCSFAβ42Aβ40Biological diagnosis

Added October 24, 2026 · DOI:10.1177/13872877261494512; PMID:42911077

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The expanded definition did not simply find more clinically typical AD. Reclassified cases had less abnormal amyloid ratios, lower tau, less neurodegeneration-marker positivity, and a much lower rate of final clinical AD diagnosis than cases positive under both systems. Biological classification therefore needs explicit clinical and longitudinal context.

Study design

Retrospective comparison of AT(N) 2018 and AA-2024 biological classifications in 146 consecutive patients evaluated for cognitive impairment at a tertiary neurology center. All had CSF Aβ42, Aβ40, Aβ42/Aβ40, phosphorylated tau, and total tau; diagnostic distributions and Cohen's kappa agreement were analyzed.

Key quantitative results

  • AT(N) 2018 classified 40/146 patients (27.4%) as biological AD, compared with 72/146 (49.3%) under AA-2024.
  • Thirty-two patients (21.9%) were reclassified, all from non-AD to AD; there were no reverse reclassifications. Agreement was moderate (κ=0.57).
  • Cases positive under both frameworks had lower Aβ42/Aβ40 and higher total tau and p-tau than reclassified cases (all p<0.001).
  • Neurodegeneration-marker positivity was 70% in concordant AD versus 25% in reclassified AD (p<0.001).
  • A final clinical AD diagnosis was assigned to 98% of concordant cases versus 38% of reclassified cases (p<0.001).

What changed

The study quantifies the real-world direction and magnitude of diagnostic expansion when AA-2024 criteria are applied to the same CSF data used for AT(N) 2018.

Strength of evidence

Moderate implementation evidence from a consecutive clinical cohort with within-patient criteria comparison. Generalizability is limited by one tertiary center, retrospective clinical adjudication, local assays/cutoffs, and the absence of longitudinal outcome validation.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

A biological AD label under AA-2024 may capture earlier or lower-tau disease but may also include patients whose presenting syndrome is not clinically attributed to AD. Criteria labels should not replace syndrome assessment or longitudinal follow-up.

Field medical relevance

Useful for explaining the operational consequences of biological definitions, the difference between amyloid positivity and clinically causal AD, and how CSF staging information modifies interpretation.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The analysis shows how a criteria change can alter classification even when the same CSF panel is used. It does not validate universal cutoffs, platform interchangeability, or a clinical decision rule for the reclassified group.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Broader biological classification could increase confirmatory testing and counseling demand, but the study evaluated neither laboratory capacity, treatment access, payer coverage, nor cost.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did AA-2024 improve diagnostic accuracy?
The study measured reclassification, not prospective diagnostic accuracy or outcomes; it cannot establish that every added case was clinically beneficial.
Were any patients moved from AD to non-AD?
No. All 32 reclassifications expanded the AD category.
Can the percentages be generalized to other clinics?
No. They depend on referral population, assays, cutoffs, and clinical adjudication.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-center study
  • Tertiary-referral population
  • Local CSF assays and cutoffs
  • No longitudinal validation of reclassified cases
  • Research criteria rather than a treatment or coverage rule

Primary source · DOI

Botelho CV, Carneiro A, Regadas C, et al. Diagnostic reclassification under the AA-2024 biological framework: A real-world comparison with ATN 2018 using cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers. J Alzheimers Dis. Published online October 22, 2026. doi:10.1177/13872877261494512.
